questions.prompt: What is the average-case time complexity of lookup, insert and delete in a hash table?

options.text: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)

questions.explanation: A good hash function with a bounded load factor spreads keys evenly, so each operation touches only a short chain or a few probes. The worst case degrades to O(n) when keys collide badly.

questions.prompt: The load factor of a hash table is defined as:

options.text: The fraction of keys that collide
The number of stored keys divided by the number of buckets
The number of buckets divided by the number of keys
The length of the longest collision chain

questions.explanation: Load factor alpha = n / m measures how full the table is. Performance degrades as it rises, which is why tables rehash into a larger array once alpha crosses a threshold.

questions.prompt: How does separate chaining resolve collisions?

options.text: It rehashes the whole table on every collision
It probes the next free bucket in the array
Each bucket holds a linked list of all keys that hash there
It rejects the colliding key

questions.explanation: Colliding keys live in a list hanging off the bucket, so the table can hold more keys than buckets. Open addressing instead stores everything in the array itself by probing.

questions.prompt: What problem is characteristic of linear probing in open addressing?

options.text: It cannot store more than one key per bucket
Primary clustering — occupied runs grow and lengthen probe sequences
It requires a linked list per bucket
It cannot detect duplicate keys

questions.explanation: Because probes step one slot at a time, contiguous occupied runs form and any key hashing into them extends the run. Quadratic probing and double hashing scatter probes to reduce this.

questions.prompt: Which is the most important property of a good hash function?

options.text: It always returns a prime number
It distributes keys uniformly across buckets
It is slow enough to be secure
It maps every key to the same bucket

questions.explanation: Uniform distribution keeps chains short and probe sequences brief, preserving the O(1) average. It should also be fast to compute and deterministic for a given key.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does a hash table lookup degrade to O(n)?

options.text: When keys are inserted in sorted order
When the table has more buckets than keys
When all keys hash to the same bucket
When the table is exactly half full

questions.explanation: If every key collides, a chained table becomes one long list and every lookup scans it. This is why an adversary who can force collisions can turn a hash table into a linear structure.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is the natural choice for testing set membership at high volume?

options.text: A stack
A linked list
A hash set
A sorted array

questions.explanation: A hash set answers 'is x present' in O(1) average time. A sorted array gives O(log n) via binary search but is costly to update; a list is O(n).

questions.prompt: When the load factor of a hash table grows too high, the usual response is to:

options.text: Delete the oldest keys
Sort the buckets
Switch the hash function to the identity
Allocate a larger table and rehash every key into it

questions.explanation: Rehashing into a bigger array restores a low load factor and short chains. It costs O(n) but happens rarely, so it is O(1) amortised per insertion — the same argument as dynamic array doubling.

questions.prompt: In open addressing, why is a deleted slot marked with a tombstone rather than simply emptied?

options.text: It keeps the table sorted
The array cannot store empty slots
Tombstones make deletion faster
An empty slot would prematurely stop a probe sequence searching for a later key

questions.explanation: A search stops at a truly empty slot. If deletion left a hole in the middle of a probe run, keys past it would become unreachable, so the slot is marked deleted-but-not-empty instead.

questions.prompt: Why is it dangerous to use a mutable object as a key in a hash table?

options.text: Mutating it changes its hash, so it can no longer be found in its bucket
Mutable keys use more memory
The table cannot compute their hash at all
It forces the table to rehash on every read

questions.explanation: The key was placed in the bucket determined by its hash at insertion. If its fields change, its hash changes, and lookups now probe the wrong bucket, leaving the entry effectively lost.
